## Lot size isn't always the deciding factor

A common instinct when preparing a subdivision file is to focus on the resulting lot size: is it big enough to be approved? That's a real criterion (the law requires a sufficient area for a viable agricultural project), but reading actual decisions shows it isn't always what decides the outcome on its own. This reading draws on [an analysis of 133 CPTAQ decisions](../133-decisions-cptaq/index.qmd).

## A file rejected, despite reasonable agricultural potential

In one of the files reviewed, a subdivision application involved residual parcels of 1.7 and 1.3 hectares. The Commission found this area too small to support a viable agricultural project, comparing production potential against well-established regional benchmarks. But a second problem compounded the first: the applicant had submitted neither a detailed project nor financial documentation to support the application. The combination — marginal area and no supporting evidence — was enough to tip the decision toward a refusal.

## A file approved, with a comparable size

In another file, two resulting properties of 40 and 36 hectares were found consistent with neighbouring properties in the area, a clear example of homogeneity. But the Commission also noted a costed agricultural project, with a specific investment in equipment, even though questions about financing remained open. The file was approved despite that grey area, precisely because economic evidence was present, even if imperfect.

## What these two files have in common

It isn't lot size alone that separates these two outcomes — it's the presence or absence of concrete economic demonstration. A file with a marginal area but a solidly costed project stands a better chance than one with ample area but no proof of viability.

## What this means for preparing a file

Before asking "is my lot size sufficient," the question to ask is "can I demonstrate, with comparable figures, that this project is agronomically viable." That proof, more than the area itself, seems to be what makes the difference in the files reviewed.

---

*Analysis based on a reading of actual CPTAQ decisions. Every file deserves an assessment suited to its own situation — the comparisons presented here are general in nature.*
